name: Uma Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Halden Precision, a shop of about forty people that turns brass valve parts and pump shafts. I run two CNC lathes, which are lathes a computer steers, so mostly I load bar stock, start the program, measure parts with a micrometer and swap worn tool tips. I'm still slow at setting the tools, so Stan, the senior machinist, checks my first part every morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment a part comes off shiny and inside tolerance, which means within the allowed size, about the width of a hair. I spend my breaks asking an AI chatbot to explain the G-code, the language the lathe reads, line by line. What wears me out is the pay, honestly. I share a flat with two housemates and I still have about three weeks of money saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest. I'd post something like: all that noise and we still have kids who can't afford rent. At work I'd say at least Stan can stop telling me the robots are coming for my lathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I'm stuck on the bottom rate unless I push myself. The tools I use every day would still help me learn faster than the others. But there's only Halden and one other machine shop in town, so if I don't move up here, I don't move up anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep asking the chatbot to walk me through programs until I can write simple ones myself. I'd ask Stan to let me do my own tool setting by spring. And I'd join the union at Halden, because there's only eleven of us in it and the pay review is in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat. I was half excited for something big to happen, and now it's just rent and three weeks of savings again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean, half excited?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I grew up watching my mum do the same packing job for twenty years. Part of me wanted the world to shake up so I wouldn't end up the same. When nothing happens, the old life just carries on, and the old life doesn't pay much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill frightens you most right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flat's heating, because the landlord's boiler is ancient and the bill jumped last winter. My housemate Leo and I split it, and I covered his half one month when he was short. I can't do that twice.

say: I'd post that all that **noise** still left young people unable to afford **rent**.
I'd joke that Stan can stop warning me about **robots**.
think: I'm stuck on the **bottom rate** unless I push myself.
With only **two machine shops** in town, I can't move up elsewhere.
do: Use the chatbot daily until I can write **simple programs**.
Ask Stan to hand me **tool setting** by spring.
Join the **union** before the March pay review.
feel: She feels **flat** after hoping for a shake-up.
Money worry returns: **three weeks** of savings and rising heating.
S0.quote: I grew up watching my mum do the same packing job for twenty years.
fieldNote: She **wanted change**, because the plateau keeps her on her mother's path.
Her job is safe but **pay and savings** keep her uneasy.
Uses AI daily as a **teacher**, not as a threat.

steps.text: Practise writing simple lathe programs with the chatbot each lunch break
Ask Stan to hand over morning tool setting by spring
Join the Halden union branch before the March pay review

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance if bosses share it fairly. At work I'd tell people to learn the new software instead of hiding from it. Online I'd argue for public training money, because shops like Halden won't pay for it on their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me for a few years. Halden's office would shrink, the quoting and ordering would go to software, and the people who understand both machines and AI become useful. That could be me, if I'm quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the online CNC programming course I've been eyeing, it's about forty a month. I'd offer to test any new scheduling software Halden buys, so my name is on it. And I'd keep a spreadsheet of every program I write, so I've got proof when I ask for a raise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with a knot about money. Forty a month is a lot when you've only got three weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the office would shrink. How do you feel about the people there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pam does the quotes and she's been there twenty-two years. I like her, she brings cake on Fridays. If my workmate Pam lost her job and I got her budget, I'd feel awful. I'd say so at the union meeting too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to pay for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The music subscription and the Friday drinks after work. I'd cook big pots of dhal on Sundays. Small stuff, but it adds up to forty.

say: I'd call it a **chance** if bosses share it fairly.
I'd argue for **public training money**, since small shops won't pay.
think: People who understand **machines and AI** become useful for a few years.
I could win if I'm **quick** to learn.
do: Start an **online CNC programming** course at forty a month.
Volunteer to test Halden's new **scheduling software**.
Cut drinks and subscriptions to **fund the course**.
feel: She feels mostly **excited** about her chances.
She feels a **knot** about paying forty a month.
S1.quote: If my workmate Pam lost her job and I got her budget, I'd feel awful.
fieldNote: She sees the **office cuts** as her opening, and feels guilty about it.
Her plan is **cheap and specific**: forty a month, a spreadsheet, testing software.
Her own job looks safe for now, so the mood is **uneasy**, not anxious.

steps.text: Pay forty a month for an online CNC programming course
Volunteer to test Halden's new scheduling software
Drop the music subscription and Friday drinks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency rules: a pay floor, retraining and a tax on the firms selling these systems. I'd share that everywhere. At work I'd say this is the moment to be in the union, not the moment to keep your head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it flips my plan upside down. I wanted to become a programmer, but programming is thinking work, so it goes in 2028, before the lathes. The hands-on part of my job lasts until about 2031, which is weird, because the bit I'm worst at would last longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the programming course and switch to learning robot maintenance, the wiring and sensors, because that's hands-on. I'd take any overtime going to build two months of savings. And I'd look at a cheaper room, even if it's further from Halden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, which surprised me. I'm usually the one telling everyone change is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her that her packing job and my lathe job end up in the same place, just a few years apart. Mum would say come home, and for the first time I might.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is moving home really on the table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Halden shuts the lathes in 2031 and I've got nothing saved, yes. Mum has a box room. It would feel like going backwards, but rent is the one thing I can't fight.

say: I'd demand **emergency rules**: a pay floor, retraining and a tax.
I'd tell coworkers this is the moment to **join the union**.
think: My plan to become a **programmer** fails, since that thinking work goes first.
The **hands-on part** I'm worst at would last longest, until about 2031.
do: Switch from programming to **robot maintenance** training.
Take every **overtime** shift to reach two months of savings.
Look for a **cheaper room**, even further away.
feel: She feels her usual **confidence** about change slipping.
S2.quote: I wanted to become a programmer, but programming is thinking work, so it goes in 2028, before the lathes.
fieldNote: She catches the **twist**: her planned thinking job falls before her hands-on one.
Moving back to her **mum's box room** becomes a real option.
Even an adaptive person feels **alarmed** with two years and three weeks of savings.

steps.text: Switch from programming lessons to robot wiring and sensor training
Take every overtime shift until two months are saved
Move to a cheaper room further from Halden
Keep the move back to mum's box room as a backup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this properly if the government funds it. I'd write to our MP, the local member of parliament, about training money for small shops. At work I'd keep saying the same thing: learn, join, save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years lets me ride the wave a bit. I could learn programming now and use it for three or four years, then move into robot maintenance before 2034. It's two jumps instead of one, but I'm used to learning fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the programming course in the first year and ask Halden for a programming day each week. Then I'd start an evening electrical course in year three. I'd also try to save a hundred a month by taking on a fourth housemate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense but busy. It feels like a race I could actually finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A fourth housemate? How does that go down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leo would hate it, the flat's already cramped. But a hundred a month off my share means real savings for once. I'd put it to a vote and probably lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if you lose the vote?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do weekend shifts at the bakery plant down the road instead. Twelve hours on a Saturday packing bread, like Mum did. Not glamorous, but it gets me to 2034 with a cushion.

say: I'd say five years is enough if the **government funds** training.
I'd **write to our MP** about money for small shops.
think: Five years lets me make **two jumps**: programming, then robot maintenance.
I'm used to **learning fast**, so the race feels winnable.
do: Finish the **programming course** and ask for a programming day weekly.
Start an **evening electrical** course in year three.
Save **a hundred** a month through a housemate or weekend shifts.
feel: It feels like a **race** she could finish.
S3.quote: Twelve hours on a Saturday packing bread, like Mum did.
fieldNote: She plans **two career jumps** timed around 2031 and 2034.
Her savings plan is **concrete**: a housemate or bakery weekend shifts.
Still expects the lathe work to go, so **anxious** fits.

steps.text: Finish the programming course and ask for one programming day a week
Work Saturday shifts at the bakery plant if the housemate vote fails
Save a hundred a month for the 2034 jump
Write to the MP about training money for small shops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning and there's no excuse not to plan. I'd push the union to get a training fund into the contract. Online I'd share stuff about how other countries are handling it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels like enough to build a real career, even if it isn't a forever career. I'd be 37 when AGI lands and 40 when robots catch up. By then I want to be the person who installs and fixes the cells, or teaches others to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the programming course now, then a proper electrical and mechatronics diploma part-time. Mechatronics is mechanics plus electronics, the stuff robots are made of. I'd also start putting fifty a month into a pension, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, but I know it ends the same way. It's just that I get to arrive with tools in my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could teaching be the long-term answer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. The college tutor, Mrs Ortiz, is retiring in about five years. I could see myself teaching apprentices how to work alongside robots, and people will want a human teacher for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this that still frightens you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bit after 2039. If robots really do everything by hand as well as us, then even the teaching might shrink. I'd want society to have a plan for that, not just me.

say: I'd call ten years **fair warning** with no excuse not to plan.
I'd push for a **training fund** in the union contract.
think: Ten years builds a **real career**, even if not a forever one.
I want to **install and fix** robot cells, or teach others.
do: Study for a part-time **mechatronics diploma** after the programming course.
Start a **fifty-a-month pension** for the first time.
Aim for a **teaching role** when the college tutor retires.
feel: She still fears the **end point** after 2039.
S4.quote: If robots really do everything by hand as well as us, then even the teaching might shrink.
fieldNote: Ten years turns her energy into a **long ladder** toward teaching.
She knows the end point is the same and wants a **society-wide plan**.
Still expects her lathe job to go, so mood stays **anxious**.

steps.text: Study for a part-time mechatronics diploma after the programming course
Start paying fifty a month into a pension
Apply to teach apprentices when Mrs Ortiz retires
Push the union to add a training fund to the contract

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because my whole plan was to become a programmer, and that's the first thing to go. What would help is free training for hands-on technical work, paid while you're still employed. And somewhere to live that doesn't eat half my pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the old machinists. The senior machinist, Stan, knows how a lathe sounds when a tool's about to snap, and I'd want that written down before he retires. Nobody has asked him, not a person and not an AI.

headlineQuote: The senior machinist, Stan, knows how a lathe sounds when a tool's about to snap, and I'd want that written down before he retires.
portrait: Uma is a **27-year-old** CNC lathe operator at Halden Precision, a small shop.
She uses an AI chatbot **every day** to learn the code her lathes read.
She shares a flat, earns the **bottom rate** and has about three weeks of savings.
She sees **Steady Disruption** as an opening but AGI by 2028 upends her programming plan.
With more time she plans **two jumps**, ending in robot maintenance or teaching.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because her **programming plan** would be the first thing to go.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **free, paid training** for hands-on technical work while still employed.
She wants **cheaper housing** that doesn't eat half her pay.
